All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

7	The requirement that the target be **triangle-free**, rather than simultaneously triangle- and pentagon-free, matters here.
8	
9	We prove both halves:
10	
11	* for every \(c>1/9\), there is a finite triangle-free universal target;
12	* for every \(c<1/9\), no such target exists.
13	
14	The proof uses two classical theorems, stated explicitly below: Szemerédi’s regularity lemma and Lovász’s theorem on the chromatic number of Kneser graphs. We do not use the recent sharp homomorphism-threshold result as a black box.
15	
16	## 1. Preliminaries
17	
18	A graph with no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\) has no closed walk of length \(3\) or \(5\): every odd closed walk contains an odd cycle of at most its length.
19	
20	Consequently, in such a graph:
21	
22	\[
23	\boxed{\text{If there is a walk of length \(3\) from \(x\) to \(y\), then }
24	N(x)\cap N(y)=\varnothing.} \tag{1}
25	\]
26	
27	Otherwise, a common neighbor would complete a closed walk of length \(5\).
28	
29	We use the following standard form of the regularity lemma.
30	
31	**Szemerédi’s regularity lemma.**  
32	For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and integer \(k_0\), there are \(M,N_0\) such that every graph on \(n\ge N_0\) vertices has a partition
33	\[
34	V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_k
35	\]
36	where \(k_0\le k\le M\), \(|V_0|\le\varepsilon n\), the other classes have the same size, and at most \(\varepsilon k^2\) unordered pairs of classes are not \(\varepsilon\)-regular.
37	
38	Here \((A,B)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-regular if
39	\[
40	|d(X,Y)-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon
41	\]
42	whenever \(X\subseteq A,Y\subseteq B\), \(|X|\ge\varepsilon|A|\), and \(|Y|\ge\varepsilon|B|\).
43	
44	---
45	
46	# 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
47	
48	Fix \(c>1/9\). Choose a positive rational number \(\tau\) with
49	\[
50	\tau<\min\left\{\frac1{100},\frac{9c-1}{1000}\right\},
51	\qquad \varepsilon=\tau^4.
52	\tag{2}
53	\]
54	
55	Let \(G\) be a \(\{C_3,C_5\}\)-free graph on sufficiently many vertices, with minimum degree at least \(cn\).
56	
57	## 2.1. A reduced graph retaining positive minimum degree
58	
59	Apply the regularity lemma with \(k_0=\lceil1/\tau\rceil\).
60	
61	Call a nonexceptional class bad if it belongs to more than \(\sqrt\varepsilon k\) irregular pairs. There are at most \(2\sqrt\varepsilon k\) bad classes. Move them into the exceptional set \(Z\).
62	
63	Write the remaining equal-sized classes as
64	\[
65	V_1,\ldots,V_\ell,\qquad |V_i|=m.
66	\]
67	Then
68	\[
69	|Z|\le(\varepsilon+2\sqrt\varepsilon)n\le3\tau^2n,
70	\qquad m\le\tau n. \tag{3}
71	\]
72	
73	Define a reduced graph \(R\) on \([\ell]\) by putting \(ij\in E(R)\) exactly when \((V_i,V_j)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-regular and has density at least \(\tau\).
74	
75	For every \(i\), averaging degrees over \(V_i\) gives
76	\[
77	cn\le |Z|+m+\tau^2km+\tau\ell m+d_R(i)m.
78	\]
79	The terms respectively allow for exceptional vertices, the class itself, irregular pairs, low-density regular pairs, and edges of \(R\). Therefore
80	\[
81	\boxed{d_R(i)m\ge(c-3\tau)n.} \tag{4}
82	\]
83	In particular, \(R\) has no isolated vertices.
84	
85	For each \(v\in V(G)\), define its support
86	\[
87	S(v)=\{i:|N(v)\cap V_i|\ge\tau m\}.
88	\]
89	Ignoring \(Z\) and the classes outside the support loses at most
90	\[
91	3\tau^2n+\tau n\le2\tau n
92	\]
93	neighbors. Thus
94	\[
95	\boxed{\sum_{i\in S(v)}|N(v)\cap V_i|\ge(c-2\tau)n.} \tag{5}
96	\]
97	In particular, every support is nonempty.
98	
99	## 2.2. Three consequences of regularity
100	
101	For a set \(S\subseteq V(R)\), write \(N_R(S)=\bigcup_{i\in S}N_R(i)\).
102	
103	We need three observations.
104	
105	**(a)** \(S(v)\) is independent in \(R\).
106	
107	Indeed, if \(ij\in E(R)\) with \(i,j\in S(v)\), regularity supplies an edge between \(N(v)\cap V_i\) and \(N(v)\cap V_j\), producing a triangle.
108	
109	**(b)** If \(a,b\) have a common neighbor, then there are no edges of \(R\) between \(S(a)\) and \(S(b)\).
110	
111	An edge between the two supports supplies an edge \(xy\), with
112	\[
113	x\in N(a),\qquad y\in N(b).
114	\]
115	Together with a common neighbor \(z\), this gives the forbidden closed walk
116	\[
117	a,x,y,b,z,a.
118	\]
119	
120	**(c)** If \(ab\in E(G)\), then
121	\[
122	\boxed{N_R(S(a))\cap N_R(S(b))=\varnothing.} \tag{6}
123	\]
124	
125	For suppose \(i\in S(a),j\in S(b)\), and \(k\) is adjacent in \(R\) to both \(i,j\). Regularity implies that all but at most \(\varepsilon m\) vertices of \(V_k\) have a neighbor in \(N(a)\cap V_i\), and likewise for \(N(b)\cap V_j\). Since \(2\varepsilon<1\), some \(y\in V_k\) has both neighbors, say \(x,z\). Then
126	\[
127	a,x,y,z,b,a
128	\]
129	is a forbidden closed walk of length \(5\).
130	
131	These arguments remain valid if some nonconsecutive vertices in a displayed walk coincide.
132	
133	## 2.3. Three finite partitions
134	
135	Partition \(V(G)\) into classes according to the vector
136	\[
137	\left(
138	\left\lfloor\frac{|N(v)\cap V_i|}{\tau m}\right\rfloor
139	\right)_{i=1}^{\ell}.
140	\]
141	Call this partition \(\mathcal P_1\). Vertices in the same class have the same support, and their neighbor densities into each \(V_i\) lie in one interval of width \(\tau\).
142	
143	Refine \(\mathcal P_1\) into \(\mathcal P_2\) by recording, for every class of \(\mathcal P_1\), whether the vertex has any neighbor in that class.
144	
145	Then refine \(\mathcal P_2\) into \(\mathcal P_3\) in the same way, recording adjacency to all classes of \(\mathcal P_2\).
146	
147	All three partitions have bounded size, independently of \(n\).
148	
149	We show that the quotient graph on \(\mathcal P_3\) is triangle-free.
150	
151	First, \(\mathcal P_1\) consists of independent sets. If adjacent vertices \(a,b\) had the same support \(S\), then (6) would give \(N_R(S)=\varnothing\), contradicting nonemptiness of \(S\) and (4). Thus the quotient has no loops.
152	
153	Suppose, for a contradiction, that three classes \(A_3,B_3,C_3\) form a triangle in the quotient. Let \(A_j,B_j,C_j\) denote their parent classes in \(\mathcal P_j\).
154	
155	Write \(S_A,S_B,S_C\) for their supports.
156	
157	### Each support occupies at least \((2c-8\tau)n\) vertices
158	
159	There is a walk of length \(3\) whose endpoints both belong to \(A_1\):
160	
161	1. start with an edge \(a_3b_3\) between \(A_3,B_3\);
162	2. because \(B_3\) has uniform neighbor-existence information about \(\mathcal P_2\), \(b_3\) has a neighbor \(c_2\in C_2\);
163	3. because \(C_2\) has uniform neighbor-existence information about \(\mathcal P_1\), \(c_2\) has a neighbor \(a_1\in A_1\).
164	
165	By (1), the two endpoints have disjoint neighborhoods.
166	
167	For each \(i\), let \(L_i\) be the lower endpoint of the density interval defining \(A_1\). The two disjoint neighborhoods give \(2L_i\le1\). Hence every vertex of \(A_1\) has neighbor density at most \(1/2+\tau\) into every \(V_i\).
168	
169	By (5),
170	\[
171	\left|\bigcup_{i\in S_A}V_i\right|
172	\ge \frac{c-2\tau}{1/2+\tau}\,n
173	\ge(2c-8\tau)n. \tag{7}
174	\]
175	The last inequality follows from
176	\[
177	(c-2\tau)-(2c-8\tau)(1/2+\tau)
178	=2\tau(1-c+4\tau)\ge0.
179	\]
180	The same holds for \(S_B,S_C\).
181	
182	### Nine units of minimum degree must fit into the graph
183	
184	Set
185	\[
186	T_A=N_R(S_A),\quad T_B=N_R(S_B),\quad T_C=N_R(S_C).
187	\]
188	
189	The actual edges between the three fine classes and (6) imply that \(T_A,T_B,T_C\) are pairwise disjoint.
190	
191	Also, there are no \(R\)-edges between any two of \(S_A,S_B,S_C\). For example, choose \(z\in C_3\). Its \(\mathcal P_3\)-signature guarantees neighbors in both \(A_2\) and \(B_2\). Those two neighbors have supports \(S_A,S_B\), so observation (b) applies.
192	
193	Thus:
194	
195	* each \(S_X\) is disjoint from every \(T_Y\);
196	* the \(S_X\) are pairwise disjoint, because a shared vertex of \(R\), having positive degree, would give an element shared by the corresponding \(T_X,T_Y\);
197	* the \(T_X\) are pairwise disjoint.
198	
199	Therefore the six unions of clusters corresponding to
200	\[
201	S_A,S_B,S_C,T_A,T_B,T_C
202	\]
203	are pairwise disjoint.
204	
205	Each \(S_X\)-union has size at least \((2c-8\tau)n\), by (7). Each \(T_X\)-union has size at least \((c-3\tau)n\), by nonemptiness of \(S_X\) and (4). Consequently,
206	\[
207	n\ge3(2c-8\tau)n+3(c-3\tau)n
208	=(9c-33\tau)n>n,
209	\]
210	by (2). This is impossible.
211	
212	The quotient on \(\mathcal P_3\) is therefore triangle-free.
213	
214	## 2.4. A single target for every \(n\)
215	
216	Let
217	\[
218	D=\lfloor1/\tau\rfloor+1.
219	\]
220	The partition sizes are bounded by
221	\[
222	b_1=D^M,\qquad b_2=b_1\,2^{b_1},\qquad b_3=b_2\,2^{b_2}.
223	\]
224	Let \(L\) exceed \(b_3\) and the regularity lemma’s threshold \(N_0\).
225	
226	Take \(H_c\) to be the disjoint union of all triangle-free graphs on at most \(L\) vertices.
227	
228	For \(n\ge N_0\), the quotient just constructed is one of its components. For \(n<N_0\), \(G\) itself is one of its components. Hence every graph under consideration maps to \(H_c\).
229	
230	This proves the upper half.
231	
232	---
233	
234	# 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
235	
236	We use the following classical theorem.
237	
238	**Lovász’s Kneser graph theorem.**  
239	The graph \(KG(m,r)\), whose vertices are the \(r\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjoint sets adjacent, has chromatic number
240	\[
241	\chi(KG(m,r))=m-2r+2
242	\qquad(m\ge2r).
243	\]
244	
245	Fix \(c<1/9\), and let \(H\) be any finite triangle-free graph, of order \(h\ge1\). We construct an admissible \(G\) that does not map to \(H\).
246	
247	Choose \(r\) sufficiently large that, with \(m=2r+h\),
248	\[
249	\frac{r}{3(m+r)}>c. \tag{8}
250	\]
251	This is possible because the left side tends to \(1/9\).
252	
253	Let
254	\[
255	F=KG(m,r).
256	\]
257	Then
258	\[
259	\chi(F)=h+2>h. \tag{9}
260	\]
261	
262	Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace every oriented edge \(x\to y\) with a path
263	\[
264	x-a_{xy}-b_{xy}-y.
265	\]
266	Call the resulting graph \(S\).
267	
268	Give its vertices a group and a label:
269	\[
270	\begin{array}{c|ccc}
271	\text{vertex}&x&a_{xy}&b_{xy}\\ \hline
272	\text{group}&0&1&2\\
273	\text{label}&x&x&y.
274	\end{array}
275	\]
276	
277	The groups form a proper \(3\)-coloring.
278	
279	We need one elementary property:
280	
281	\[
282	\boxed{\begin{minipage}{0.84\linewidth}
283	If a length-three walk in \(S\) has endpoints in the same group, then their labels are adjacent in \(F\), and hence are disjoint \(r\)-subsets of \([m]\).
284	\end{minipage}} \tag{10}
285	\]
286	
287	For group \(0\), such a walk traverses one subdivided edge. For group \(1\), its possible group sequences are \(1,0,2,1\) and \(1,2,0,1\); direct inspection gives adjacent labels. Group \(2\) is symmetric.
288	
289	Now choose an integer \(t\). For each group \(j\in\{0,1,2\}\), introduce independent sets
290	\[
291	A_j=[m]\times[t],\qquad |B_j|=rt,
292	\]
293	and join \(A_j\) completely to \(B_j\).
294	
295	For every vertex \(v\in S\) in group \(j\), with label \(X\in\binom{[m]}r\), join \(v\) to
296	\[
297	X\times[t]\subseteq A_j.
298	\]
299	Keep all edges of \(S\), and add no others. Call the resulting graph \(G_t\).
300	
301	Every vertex has degree at least \(rt\), and
302	\[
303	|G_t|=|S|+3(m+r)t.
304	\]
305	By (8), sufficiently large \(t\) gives
306	\[
307	\delta(G_t)\ge rt>c|G_t|. \tag{11}
308	\]
309	
310	## 3.1. There are no triangles or pentagons
311	
312	Delete the edges of \(S\). The remaining graph is the disjoint union of three bipartite graphs, one for each group. In each, all vertices of \(S\) lie on the same side.
313	
314	An odd cycle of length at most \(5\) must therefore use an odd number of edges of \(S\).
315	
316	* **One edge of \(S\):** impossible, since its endpoints belong to different group-components after the edges of \(S\) are deleted.
317	* **Three edges of \(S\):** a triangle is impossible inside \(S\). A pentagon would consist of a length-three walk in \(S\), plus two edges through some \(A_j\). Its endpoints have the same group and share a coordinate of their labels, contradicting (10).
318	* **Five edges of \(S\):** impossible, since subdividing every edge into a three-edge path gives \(S\) no cycle shorter than \(9\).
319	
320	Thus \(G_t\) contains neither a triangle nor a pentagon.
321	
322	## 3.2. There is no homomorphism to \(H\)
323	
324	Suppose \(f:G_t\to H\) existed. For each edge \(xy\) of \(F\), its subdivision gives a length-three walk in \(H\) from \(f(x)\) to \(f(y)\).
325	
326	If \(f(x)=f(y)\), that would be a closed walk of length \(3\), impossible in a triangle-free graph. Hence \(f\), restricted to the original vertices of \(F\), is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors. This contradicts (9).
327	
328	Since \(H\) was arbitrary, no \(c<1/9\) has the required property.
329	
330	Combining the two halves proves the claimed infimum.
331	
332	---
333	
334	# 4. Executable checks
335	
336	The following Python performs actual finite checks, rather than merely printing the asserted answer. It:
337	
338	* materializes examples of the lower-bound construction;
339	* exhaustively checks their triangles, pentagons, and the crucial label property (10);
340	* uses Z3 to check the Kneser chromatic numbers in those examples;
341	* checks the triangle-free length-three-walk obstruction on all 173 triangle-free graphs in NetworkX’s graph atlas;
342	* exactly checks regularity certificates for sample blow-ups, constructs the three partitions in the upper-bound proof, and verifies the resulting homomorphisms;
343	* computes obstruction parameters using exact rational and integer arithmetic;
344	* checks the polynomial identities used in the constant estimates.
345	
346	The infinite assertions are proved above; finite testing is not being substituted for them.

29	**Szemerédi’s regularity lemma.**  
30	For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and integer \(k_0\), there are \(M,N_0\) such that every graph on \(n\ge N_0\) vertices has a partition
31	\[
32	V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_k

37	\[
38	|d(X,Y)-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon

40	whenever \(X\subseteq A,Y\subseteq B\), \(|X|\ge\varepsilon|A|\), and \(|Y|\ge\varepsilon|B|\).

232	# 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
233	
234	We use the following classical theorem.
235	
236	**Lovász’s Kneser graph theorem.**  
237	The graph \(KG(m,r)\), whose vertices are the \(r\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjoint sets adjacent, has chromatic number
238	\[
239	\chi(KG(m,r))=m-2r+2
240	\qquad(m\ge2r).
241	\]
242	
243	Fix \(c<1/9\), and let \(H\) be any finite triangle-free graph, of order \(h\ge1\). We construct an admissible \(G\) that does not map to \(H\).
244	
245	Choose \(r\) sufficiently large that, with \(m=2r+h\),
246	\[
247	\frac{r}{3(m+r)}>c. \tag{8}
248	\]
249	This is possible because the left side tends to \(1/9\).
250	
251	Let
252	\[
253	F=KG(m,r).
254	\]
255	Then
256	\[
257	\chi(F)=h+2>h. \tag{9}
258	\]
259	
260	Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace every oriented edge \(x\to y\) with a path
261	\[
262	x-a_{xy}-b_{xy}-y.
263	\]
264	Call the resulting graph \(S\).
265	
266	Give its vertices a group and a label:
267	\[
268	\begin{array}{c|ccc}
269	\text{vertex}&x&a_{xy}&b_{xy}\\ \hline
270	\text{group}&0&1&2\\
271	\text{label}&x&x&y.
272	\end{array}
273	\]
274	
275	The groups form a proper \(3\)-coloring.
276	
277	We need one elementary property:
278	
279	\[
280	\boxed{\begin{minipage}{0.84\linewidth}
281	If a length-three walk in \(S\) has endpoints in the same group, then their labels are adjacent in \(F\), and hence are disjoint \(r\)-subsets of \([m]\).
282	\end{minipage}} \tag{10}
283	\]
284	
285	For group \(0\), such a walk traverses one subdivided edge. For group \(1\), its possible group sequences are \(1,0,2,1\) and \(1,2,0,1\); direct inspection gives adjacent labels. Group \(2\) is symmetric.
286	
287	Now choose an integer \(t\). For each group \(j\in\{0,1,2\}\), introduce independent sets
288	\[
289	A_j=[m]\times[t],\qquad |B_j|=rt,
290	\]
291	and join \(A_j\) completely to \(B_j\).
292	
293	For every vertex \(v\in S\) in group \(j\), with label \(X\in\binom{[m]}r\), join \(v\) to
294	\[
295	X\times[t]\subseteq A_j.
296	\]
297	Keep all edges of \(S\), and add no others. Call the resulting graph \(G_t\).
298	
299	Every vertex has degree at least \(rt\), and
300	\[
301	|G_t|=|S|+3(m+r)t.
302	\]
303	By (8), sufficiently large \(t\) gives
304	\[
305	\delta(G_t)\ge rt>c|G_t|. \tag{11}
306	\]
307	
308	## 3.1. There are no triangles or pentagons
309	
310	Delete the edges of \(S\). The remaining graph is the disjoint union of three bipartite graphs, one for each group. In each, all vertices of \(S\) lie on the same side.
311	
312	An odd cycle of length at most \(5\) must therefore use an odd number of edges of \(S\).
313	
314	* **One edge of \(S\):** impossible, since its endpoints belong to different group-components after the edges of \(S\) are deleted.
315	* **Three edges of \(S\):** a triangle is impossible inside \(S\). A pentagon would consist of a length-three walk in \(S\), plus two edges through some \(A_j\). Its endpoints have the same group and share a coordinate of their labels, contradicting (10).
316	* **Five edges of \(S\):** impossible, since subdividing every edge into a three-edge path gives \(S\) no cycle shorter than \(9\).
317	
318	Thus \(G_t\) contains neither a triangle nor a pentagon.
319	
320	## 3.2. There is no homomorphism to \(H\)
321	
322	Suppose \(f:G_t\to H\) existed. For each edge \(xy\) of \(F\), its subdivision gives a length-three walk in \(H\) from \(f(x)\) to \(f(y)\).
323	
324	If \(f(x)=f(y)\), that would be a closed walk of length \(3\), impossible in a triangle-free graph. Hence \(f\), restricted to the original vertices of \(F\), is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors. This contradicts (9).
325	
326	Since \(H\) was arbitrary, no \(c<1/9\) has the required property.
327	
328	Combining the two halves proves the claimed infimum.
